Instructions to candidates: Answer FOUR questions chosen from any ONE SECTION ONLY. All questions carry equal marks.

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.

Section ATR (Q13-18) : généralités tirées des auteurs classiques du programme (Mbiti en particulier : « I am because we are... », « living-dead ») ; les croyances varient selon les peuples et le corrigé le dit. questions.corrige_markdown: An Imam is a leader in Islam. In its most common use the word means the person who stands in front and leads the congregation in the ritual prayer (salat); he is usually the one most knowledgeable in the Quran and the rules of prayer. The word also describes a religious leader and scholar of a community or mosque, who preaches the Friday sermon, teaches, advises and may officiate at weddings and funerals. In a wider historical sense it can refer to the head of the Muslim community (the caliph). In Shia Islam the term has a special meaning, referring to the divinely guided successors of the Prophet from the line of Ali. The title is also given as an honour to great scholars, such as the founders of the schools of law.
themes: A Level Religious Studies - imamate and leadership in islam

questions.enonce_markdown:
Can one become a faithful Muslim without an Imam?

(20 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** The answer depends on what is meant by "Imam" and on which Muslim tradition is considered. In the mainstream Sunni understanding, a person becomes and remains a faithful Muslim without needing an imam as an intermediary. In Shia teaching the imamate has a different place.

**1. Why one can be a faithful Muslim without an Imam (Sunni view).**
(i) *Faith is personal.* A person becomes a Muslim by sincerely declaring the shahada ("there is no god but Allah and Muhammad is the messenger of Allah") and believing in it. No priest or imam is needed to confer the faith.
(ii) *Direct relationship with Allah.* There is no priesthood or clergy in Islam, and no human intermediary between the believer and Allah. Each person is responsible for his or her own deeds.
(iii) *The pillars can be fulfilled individually.* Prayer may be performed alone at home, fasting, zakat and hajj are personal duties; the Quran and the Sunnah are available to every believer.
(iv) *The imam is not infallible.* He is a leader in prayer and a teacher, who may be replaced; any knowledgeable Muslim may lead the prayer.

**2. Why an imam is nevertheless useful.**
(i) Congregational prayer, which Muslims value highly, requires someone to lead it, as do the Friday prayer and its sermon, the festival prayers and the funeral prayer.
(ii) The imam teaches the Quran, explains the rules of religion and advises, so that people do not fall into error.
(iii) He guides the community, presides at weddings, naming ceremonies and burials, and helps keep unity.
(iv) A Muslim who has no access to teaching is likely to find it difficult to fulfil all duties properly.

**3. The Shia view.** In Twelver Shia teaching, belief in the imamate (the divinely guided leadership of Ali and his descendants) is part of the principles of faith. For Shia Muslims, then, a rightly guided imam holds a necessary place in religion. Sunni Muslims do not share this belief and consider the caliphate or leadership of the community a matter of public interest.

**Conclusion.** In the Sunni understanding a Muslim can be faithful without an imam, because faith and the five pillars depend on the individual's relationship with Allah, but an imam is useful for leading congregational worship and for teaching. Shia Muslims hold a different view in which the imamate is part of the faith.
themes: A Level Religious Studies - imamate and leadership in islam
